Title: Qualified Person Training
Description: This instructor-led course teaches employees how to recognize electrical hazards, assess risk, and apply safe work practices in accordance with OSHA, MSHA, and NFPA 70E. Participants will gain the knowledge and skills required to be designated as a Qualified Person under GSL Electric’s Electrical Safety Program.
LongDescription:
Qualified Person Training (Instructor-Led)

The Qualified Person Training course is an instructor-led program designed to prepare GSL Electric employees to safely perform electrical work on or near energized equipment in accordance with OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart K, MSHA §56.12001–§56.12071, and the NFPA 70E Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace. This training fulfills GSL Electric’s requirements for designating employees as Qualified Persons as defined in the company’s Electrical Safety Program.

Through classroom instruction, demonstrations, and discussion, participants will gain a deep understanding of electrical hazards—including shock, arc flash, and arc blast risks—and learn the essential practices and procedures to mitigate them. The training emphasizes safe work practices, hazard identification, and compliance with the hierarchy of risk control methods to reduce potential injury or damage to health.

Participants will learn to:

  • Identify exposed energized electrical conductors and circuit parts and determine nominal system voltages.

  • Establish and maintain Limited, Restricted, and Arc Flash Boundaries as required by NFPA 70E.

  • Select and properly use personal protective equipment (PPE), insulated tools, and testing instruments rated for the voltage and energy level.

  • Perform electrical shock and arc flash risk assessments, including required documentation and job safety planning.

  • Understand and apply the procedures for energized electrical work, including the Energized Work Permit process, pre-task assessments, and lockout/tagout verification.

  • Coordinate with Isolation Officers, Foremen, and the Safety Department to ensure work is performed in an electrically safe work condition whenever possible.

The course also covers the responsibilities of Qualified and Authorized Persons, including decision-making authority, risk evaluation, and communication with host employers during energized work tasks. Participants will review incident response procedures and methods for emergency release in the event of an electrical contact.

Upon successful completion, employees will demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and decision-making ability necessary to meet GSL Electric’s definition of a Qualified Person. Training completion will be documented by the Safety Department and maintained in the employee’s training record in accordance with NFPA 70E 110.4 and company policy.

LongDescription:
Qualified Person Training (Instructor-Led)

The Qualified Person Training course is an instructor-led program designed to prepare GSL Electric employees to safely perform electrical work on or near energized equipment in accordance with OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart K, MSHA §56.12001–§56.12071, and the NFPA 70E Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace. This training fulfills GSL Electric’s requirements for designating employees as Qualified Persons as defined in the company’s Electrical Safety Program.

Through classroom instruction, demonstrations, and discussion, participants will gain a deep understanding of electrical hazards—including shock, arc flash, and arc blast risks—and learn the essential practices and procedures to mitigate them. The training emphasizes safe work practices, hazard identification, and compliance with the hierarchy of risk control methods to reduce potential injury or damage to health.

Participants will learn to:

  • Identify exposed energized electrical conductors and circuit parts and determine nominal system voltages.

  • Establish and maintain Limited, Restricted, and Arc Flash Boundaries as required by NFPA 70E.

  • Select and properly use personal protective equipment (PPE), insulated tools, and testing instruments rated for the voltage and energy level.

  • Perform electrical shock and arc flash risk assessments, including required documentation and job safety planning.

  • Understand and apply the procedures for energized electrical work, including the Energized Work Permit process, pre-task assessments, and lockout/tagout verification.

  • Coordinate with Isolation Officers, Foremen, and the Safety Department to ensure work is performed in an electrically safe work condition whenever possible.

The course also covers the responsibilities of Qualified and Authorized Persons, including decision-making authority, risk evaluation, and communication with host employers during energized work tasks. Participants will review incident response procedures and methods for emergency release in the event of an electrical contact.

Upon successful completion, employees will demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and decision-making ability necessary to meet GSL Electric’s definition of a Qualified Person. Training completion will be documented by the Safety Department and maintained in the employee’s training record in accordance with NFPA 70E 110.4 and company policy.

LongDescription:
Safety Inspections 

Regular inspections are a cornerstone of GSL Electric’s safety program. They ensure that tools, equipment, and work areas are safe, hazards are identified and corrected, and compliance with OSHA, MSHA, and company requirements is maintained. This course provides Safety Coordinators, Foremen, and employees with the knowledge and responsibilities needed to carry out effective safety inspections and keep accurate records.

What You’ll Learn

  • Roles & Responsibilities: Understanding the inspection duties of Foremen, Safety Coordinators, project leadership, and employees—including daily visual checks and tagging defective equipment out of service.

  • Work Area Inspections: How to perform daily jobsite safety observations, correct unsafe behaviors immediately, and document conditions using checklists and inspection forms.

  • Pre-Operation Equipment Inspections: Requirements for vehicles, manlifts, forklifts, aerial and scissor lifts, and other mobile equipment under both OSHA and MSHA standards.

  • Quarterly & Monthly Inspections: Procedures for inspecting electrical tools and cords, fire extinguishers, fall protection equipment, and maintaining proper records for one year.

  • Scaffold Inspections: The role of competent persons in performing and documenting daily scaffold inspections to ensure safety and regulatory compliance.

  • Employee Responsibilities: Daily pre-use inspections of tools, extension cords, ladders, harnesses, lanyards, and all personal protective equipment.

Why It Matters

Inspections are not just a regulatory requirement—they are a proactive way to prevent accidents, extend the life of equipment, and protect employees from harm. Documenting inspections creates accountability, demonstrates compliance, and protects both the company and its workforce. By performing thorough inspections and maintaining accurate records, Safety Coordinators and project leaders help ensure that every employee can work with safe tools, equipment, and conditions—and return home safely at the end of the day.

LongDescription:
Injury & Incident Investigations

Thorough and effective investigations are a cornerstone of GSL Electric’s safety program. When injuries or incidents occur, it is the responsibility of Foremen and Safety Coordinators to gather the facts, determine the causes, and identify corrective actions that will prevent similar events from happening again. This course provides step-by-step guidance on how to conduct investigations that go beyond simply filling out forms and instead create real improvements in workplace safety.

What You’ll Learn

  • Purpose of Investigations: Why investigations are used to prevent recurrence, not assign blame, while still ensuring disciplinary action is taken if safety violations are discovered.

  • Immediate Response: How to prioritize employee medical needs, secure the scene, and take steps to prevent additional hazards after an incident.

  • Evidence Collection: Methods for documenting the scene with photos, sketches, and notes, as well as gathering written witness statements and preserving key details before conditions change.

  • Incident Reporting: Procedures for notifying the Safety Department, Project Managers, clients, and regulatory agencies, and the importance of submitting reports and evidence within required timelines.

  • Interviewing & Fact Gathering: Techniques for asking the right questions, reviewing equipment and PPE use, and identifying both unsafe conditions and behaviors that contributed to the incident.

  • Root Cause Analysis & Corrective Actions: How to identify the underlying factors of incidents and determine effective steps to prevent recurrence.

Title: Qualified Person - Required Precautions & Practices / Energized Work
Description: This course reviews G.S.L. Learners will understand how to assess risk, maintain compliance with NEC and NFPA 70E, and respond to electrical emergencies effectively. Designed for Qualified and Authorized personnel engaged in energized work.
LongDescription:
This training course provides a detailed overview of G.S.L. Electric’s Energized Work Policy and Procedures, ensuring all employees understand and apply the required precautions when performing work on or near energized electrical equipment. Through a series of guided scenes, learners will review critical safety standards, hazard identification processes, and compliance expectations aligned with NFPA 70E and NEC requirements.

The course begins with a review of energized work barriers and protective measures, emphasizing the correct use of rubber insulating equipment, voltage-rated plastic guards, and mechanical barriers to maintain safe approach boundaries. Learners will then explore the documentation and verification requirements that must be completed prior to any energized work — including client coordination, hazard recognition, risk assessment, and the completion of G.S.L.’s Energized Work Permit.

Subsequent sections reinforce the importance of proper PPE selection, inspection, and use, the establishment of arc flash and shock boundaries, and the prohibition of conductive materials within restricted areas. Participants will also learn the proper procedures for tool inspection, safe equipment handling, and incident energy level verification to ensure compliance with G.S.L. and regulatory standards.

Finally, the course outlines the emergency response procedures for electrical shock and arc flash incidents, including required safety equipment staging (fire extinguisher, first aid kit, AED, and communication devices) and immediate response steps in the event of an electrical injury.

Learning Objectives:

Upon successful completion of this course, participants will be able to:

  • Identify and apply the required precautions for energized work under G.S.L. Electric policy.

  • Demonstrate proper use and inspection of barriers, tools, and PPE.

  • Perform pre-task risk assessments and complete the G.S.L. Energized Work Permit.

  • Maintain compliance with NEC and NFPA 70E safety requirements.

Title: Safety Coordinator - 11.0 OSHA & MSHA Inspections
Description:
Course Description – OSHA & MSHA Inspections
This course explains the rights and responsibilities of employers, employees, and Safety Coordinators during OSHA and MSHA inspections. You’ll learn how inspections are conducted, what triggers them, and how to respond to citations, penalties, and abatement requirements. The training also covers posting requirements, inspection priorities, and the role of Safety Coordinators in ensuring hazards are corrected quickly, documentation is accurate, and crews remain safe and compliant.
LongDescription:
OSHA & MSHA Inspections

Understanding how OSHA and MSHA inspections work is critical for Safety Coordinators, Foremen, and project leadership at GSL Electric. This course explains inspection procedures, employer and employee responsibilities, and the steps required to correct hazards, manage citations, and maintain compliance with federal safety laws.

What You’ll Learn

  • OSHA Overview: The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 requires employers to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards and empowers OSHA to inspect, cite, and penalize violations.

  • Inspection Procedures: What to expect during unannounced OSHA inspections—including entry, scope, records review, and closing conferences—as well as employer and employee rights during inspections.

  • Inspection Priorities: How OSHA prioritizes imminent danger situations, fatalities, severe injuries, worker complaints, referrals, targeted inspections, and follow-up inspections.

  • Imminent Danger: How OSHA defines imminent danger, what conditions qualify, and the role of Safety Coordinators in reporting and addressing hazards immediately.

  • Citations & Penalties: How violations are classified (willful, serious, repeated, and other-than-serious), maximum penalty amounts, abatement deadlines, and posting requirements for OSHA Notices.

  • Employer & Employee Rights: Options for informal conferences, petitions for modification of abatement dates, alternate standards, and the ability for employees to raise objections.

  • MSHA Inspections: Requirements under the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977, including inspection frequency, citation procedures, penalties, and closure orders for unsafe conditions on mine projects.

  • Safety Coordinator Responsibilities: The critical role Safety Coordinators play in inspections—ensuring hazards are corrected quickly, documentation is accurate, corrective actions are taken, and findings are communicated across crews and management.

Why It Matters

OSHA and MSHA inspections are designed to protect workers by ensuring hazards are identified and corrected promptly. Failing to comply can result in severe penalties, work stoppages, and risks to employee safety. By understanding how inspections are conducted and how to respond effectively, Safety Coordinators and project leadership protect employees, maintain compliance, and uphold GSL Electric’s reputation for safety and accountability.

For GSL Electric to operate safely and fairly, all employees must follow established safety rules and work standards. This course explains GSL Electric’s progressive disciplinary system, its purpose, and the roles of Foremen and Safety Coordinators in applying discipline consistently, fairly, and effectively.

  • The Purpose of Discipline: Why discipline is used to correct behavior, not punish, and how it helps prevent accidents, protect employees, and reinforce accountability.

  • Roles & Responsibilities: The Foreman’s primary role in disciplining crew members, and the Safety Coordinator’s responsibility to ensure proper steps, documentation, and signatures are completed.

  • Consistency & Fairness: Why it’s critical that discipline is applied equally to all employees, including supervisors, to maintain credibility and trust.

  • Timing & Approach: How discipline should be timely, constructive, and preferably delivered in the work area to correct unsafe actions before they result in an accident.

  • Record Management: How documentation is submitted to the Safety Director and Human Resources, and how violations may be removed from an employee’s record after a year of compliance.

Why It Matters

Disciplinary action is a proactive tool for keeping employees safe, ensuring compliance, and maintaining operational efficiency. By applying progressive discipline in a consistent and documented way, Foremen and Safety Coordinators not only protect employees and crews but also reinforce GSL Electric’s culture of safety and fairness. Ultimately, the goal is not punishment, but improvement—helping employees correct unsafe behaviors and ensuring everyone can return home safely at the end of the day.

Title: Qualified Person - 2024 NFPA 70E Required Boundaries
Description: This course explains shock risk assessments and shock protection approach boundaries in accordance with the 2024 NFPA 70E, including requirements for qualified, authorized, and unqualified personnel working near energized electrical conductors and circuit parts.
LongDescription:
This online training provides an overview of electrical shock hazard protection as defined by the 2024 NFPA 70E Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace. The course explains how a shock risk assessment is used to determine voltage exposure, establish approach boundaries, and identify the personal protective equipment necessary to minimize the risk of electric shock.

Learners will review the purpose and application of the limited approach boundary and restricted approach boundary, including how these boundaries apply when personnel are working near exposed energized electrical conductors or circuit parts. The training also explains the use of NFPA 70E Table 130.4(E)(a) for AC systems and Table 130.4(E)(b) for DC systems.

In addition, the course outlines restrictions for unqualified persons, required alerting methods when working near approach boundaries, and escort requirements when an unqualified person must cross the limited approach boundary. The conditions under which qualified and authorized persons may approach within the restricted approach boundary are also addressed, including insulation and guarding requirements.

This training is intended to reinforce safe work practices, regulatory compliance, and clear understanding of shock protection boundaries when energized electrical work cannot be avoided.
Tags: Qualified Person; NFPA 70E; Shock Protection Boundaries

Title: Permit-Required Confined Spaces
Description: Confined spaces present unique and serious hazards that require specific safety measures to protect anyone entering them. Whether it’s a tank, manhole, or pit, these spaces are not designed for continuous occupancy and can pose significant risks, such as hazardous atmospheres, engulfment, or other critical dangers.
LongDescription: Confined spaces present unique and serious hazards that require specific safety measures to protect anyone entering them. Whether it’s a tank, manhole, or pit, these spaces are not designed for continuous occupancy and can pose significant risks, such as hazardous atmospheres, engulfment, or other critical dangers. To safeguard employees, it is crucial to understand the difference between a confined space and a Permit-Required Confined Space (PRCS). A PRCS typically has life-threatening hazards like toxic gases, or potential for entrapment, and requires strict safety protocols under OSHA regulations. With proper training, careful oversight, and a robust permit system, we can ensure every confined space entry is performed safely and in compliance with regulatory standards.
Tags: Reporting; Safety; Hazards; Communication; OSHA

Title: Qualified Person - Arc Flash Personal Protective Equipment
Description: This course provides an overview of arc flash hazard awareness and PPE selection in accordance with the 2024 NFPA 70E and GSL’s Electrical Safety Program. Learners will review incident energy labeling, and proper use of 8 cal/cm² and 40 cal/cm² arc flash kits to ensure safe and compliant energized work practices.
LongDescription:
This course provides detailed training on arc flash hazards, incident energy labeling, and the proper selection and use of arc flash personal protective equipment (PPE) in accordance with the 2024 NFPA 70E and GSL’s Electrical Safety Program. The course is designed for employees who may plan, supervise, or perform work on or near energized electrical equipment where arc flash hazards may be present.

Learners will gain an understanding of how incident energy is calculated and displayed on equipment labels, how working distance affects exposure, and how this information is used to determine PPE requirements. The training explains GSL’s use of the NFPA 70E simplified method for arc flash PPE selection, including when to use an 8 cal/cm² arc flash kit and when a 40 cal/cm² arc flash kit is required based on incident energy exposure.

The course also addresses critical limitations related to high incident energy levels. Participants will learn that when equipment labels indicate incident energy exposures exceeding 40 cal/cm², equipment covers must not be removed, and the circuit must be de-energized and controlled using Lockout/Tagout procedures before work can proceed. Additional topics include PPE inspection requirements, proper care, storage, and maintenance of arc-rated clothing, and the responsibilities of employees to follow established boundaries and safety controls.

By the end of this course, learners will be able to interpret arc flash equipment labels, select appropriate PPE, recognize when energized work is prohibited, and apply GSL’s Electrical Safety Program requirements to reduce the risk of arc flash and electrical shock injuries while maintaining compliance with NFPA 70E.
Tags: Safety; Arc Flash; PPE; NFPA 70E

  • Implement safety protocols. Use proper equipment, techniques, and OSHA-compliant measures to mitigate risks.
  • Use personal protective equipment. Wearing appropriate PPE like harnesses and high-visibility vests minimizes injury risks.
  • Conduct regular inspections. Checking safety equipment and work areas ensures a safe environment.
  • Encourage a safety culture. Empower workers to prioritize safety and report unsafe conditions.
  • Stay informed about hazards. Learn from real-life examples and statistics to understand risks and prevention strategies.
  • Communicate effectively. Maintain clear communication to address safety concerns and prevent accidents.
By applying these safety principles, you can help create a safer work environment and reduce the risk of workplace injuries and fatalities.

The training emphasizes consistent reporting, effective case management, and return-to-work practices that protect employee health, meet regulatory requirements, and prevent future injuries.
LongDescription:
Injury & Case Management

At GSL Electric, accident prevention is our highest priority, but when an injury does occur, it must be handled quickly, consistently, and in compliance with safety regulations. This course provides Foremen, Safety Coordinators, and employees with the knowledge and procedures necessary to properly respond to injuries, deliver first aid, and manage cases from initial treatment through return-to-work.

What You’ll Learn

  • First Aid & Emergency Action: How to stay calm, assess the scene, check responsiveness and breathing, control bleeding, and protect yourself while assisting injured employees.

  • Life-Threatening Emergencies: Recognizing when to request trained medical professionals for conditions such as unconsciousness, severe bleeding, electrical shock, or suspected spinal injuries.

  • Incident Response Procedures: Following site-specific emergency communication plans, securing the scene, and reporting injuries according to company and regulatory requirements.

  • Minor Injuries: Providing proper first aid, submitting notifications, completing reports, and ensuring the injury does not worsen during recovery.

  • Serious Injuries: Coordinating immediate care, transporting employees to approved medical facilities, and ensuring a Foreman or Safety Coordinator interfaces with the treating physician.

  • Return-to-Work Policy: Working with medical professionals to support full-duty return when possible or assigning light-duty work as needed to reduce lost time and support recovery.

  • Case Management & Documentation: Submitting injury reports to the Safety Director within 24 hours, maintaining up-to-date records, and ensuring consistent handling of all injuries.

Why It Matters

Timely and accurate injury management protects the health and well-being of employees while reducing risks and liabilities for the company. By documenting injuries properly, coordinating medical care, and reinforcing return-to-work practices, GSL Electric ensures compliance with OSHA requirements, consistency across all projects, and a safer workplace for everyone. Most importantly, proper case management supports our commitment to “Zero Broken Lives” by making sure every employee gets the care they need and returns home safely.

Title: Qualified Person - Electrical Shock & Arc Flash Risk Assessments (Safety-Related Work Practices)
Description: This course provides an overview of safety-related work practices required when performing energized electrical work in accordance with the 2024 NFPA 70E. Learners will review qualification requirements, energized work permits, electric shock and arc flash risk assessments, and the hierarchy of risk control methods. The course also explains how to document risk assessments and select appropriate protective measures to reduce the likelihood and severity of electrical injuries.
LongDescription:
This course delivers a comprehensive overview of safety-related work practices required when employees are exposed to energized electrical conductors and circuit parts, in alignment with the 2024 NFPA 70E standard. It is designed to reinforce the critical requirements that must be followed when electrical equipment operating at 50 volts or greater cannot be placed in an electrically safe work condition and energized work is permitted.

Participants will learn the conditions under which energized electrical work may be performed, including the roles and responsibilities of Qualified and Authorized persons, the requirement for an energized electrical work permit, and the completion of both electric shock and arc flash risk assessments. The course explains how to identify electrical hazards, evaluate the likelihood and severity of potential injuries, and determine when additional protective measures are necessary.

The training also covers the hierarchy of risk control methods—elimination, substitution, engineering controls, awareness, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment—and emphasizes the importance of applying the most effective controls whenever possible. Learners will gain an understanding of how human error can impact electrical safety and how risk assessments must address its potential consequences on personnel, equipment, and the work environment.

In addition, the course outlines documentation requirements for shock and arc flash risk assessments, including voltage exposure, approach boundaries, arc flash boundaries, and PPE selection. It highlights key factors that influence arc flash risk, such as equipment design, overcurrent protection, operating condition, and maintenance status. Finally, the course clarifies the roles of Project Managers, Foremen, Qualified and Authorized persons, and the Safety Department in planning, reviewing, and approving energized work to ensure consistent, compliant, and safe electrical operations.

Title: Qualified Person - Workplace Inspections, Pre-Task Assessments, Briefings
Description: This course reviews G.S.L. Electric’s Electrical Hazard Assessment and Safe Work Practices. Learners will understand how to identify and control electrical hazards, complete job safety plans, perform NFPA 70E-compliant risk assessments, and implement proper lockout/tagout and GFCI protection. The training reinforces safe work procedures around energized, overhead, and underground systems to prevent electrical incidents and ensure regulatory compliance.
LongDescription:
This course provides a comprehensive review of G.S.L. Electric’s procedures for electrical hazard assessment and safe work planning in accordance with the 2024 NFPA 70E and OSHA requirements. It emphasizes the responsibilities of Foremen, Safety Coordinators, and Qualified Employees in identifying, evaluating, and controlling electrical hazards on active job sites.

Through step-by-step instruction, learners will understand how to assess work areas for energized conductors and circuit parts operating at 50 volts or more, establish an electrically safe work condition, and properly document job safety planning requirements. The training also covers the creation and review of Job Safety Plans, including task descriptions, hazard identification, electric shock and arc flash risk assessments, and emergency response procedures.

Participants will learn the importance of conducting job briefings, performing pre-task assessments, and implementing appropriate hazard controls such as lockout/tagout (LOTO) procedures. Additional focus is placed on the safe handling of overhead and underground utilities, maintaining safe approach distances, and preventing unintentional contact with energized parts through the use of barriers, guarding, and insulation.

The course concludes with instruction on GFCI protection requirements and the procedures for reporting and investigating electrical incidents to ensure continuous improvement in safety performance.

Learning Objectives:

After completing this course, learners will be able to:

  • Identify and assess electrical hazards associated with voltages of 50 volts or greater.

  • Develop and document a compliant Job Safety Plan before performing electrical work.

  • Perform and document electric shock and arc flash risk assessments in accordance with NFPA 70E.

  • Implement hazard controls, including lockout/tagout, guarding, and GFCI protection.

  • Recognize and follow safe work practices around overhead and underground utilities.

  • Respond appropriately to electrical incidents and understand investigation requirements.

Title: Safety Coordinator - 4.0 Task Training
Description: This course teaches Safety Coordinators how to provide, observe, and document task training to ensure employees work safely, competently, and in compliance with OSHA and MSHA standards.
LongDescription:
Task Training 

Task training is one of the most important responsibilities of a Safety Coordinator. This course provides the knowledge and tools you need to ensure employees are properly trained, closely supervised, and officially documented before performing any new job or operating equipment.

What You’ll Learn

  • The Safety Coordinator’s Role: How task training protects you, your crew, and the company by combining clear instructions with documented proof of training.

  • Skill Level Assessment: Why you must never assume an employee is qualified until their abilities are evaluated.

  • Step-by-Step Instruction: Best practices for preparing employees to learn, presenting tasks clearly, reviewing hazards, and confirming understanding by having employees repeat back instructions.

  • Observation & Coaching: How to monitor employees in both non-productive and productive environments, provide corrective feedback in a positive way, and taper off supervision as competence grows.

  • Documentation Requirements: The importance of using GSL’s Task Training forms, including the Certificate of Task Training, to create accountability, maintain compliance with OSHA and MSHA, and demonstrate that all training was conducted properly.

Why It Matters

Proper task training prevents accidents, improves craftsmanship, and ensures regulatory compliance. More importantly, it reinforces GSL Electric’s commitment to safety and our philosophy of “Zero Broken Lives.” Documenting every training session not only protects the company, but also provides proof that employees have the knowledge and support they need to succeed.

Title: Qualified Person Training
Description: This instructor-led course teaches employees how to recognize electrical hazards, assess risk, and apply safe work practices in accordance with OSHA, MSHA, and NFPA 70E. Participants will gain the knowledge and skills required to be designated as a Qualified Person under GSL Electric’s Electrical Safety Program.
LongDescription:
Qualified Person Training (Instructor-Led)

The Qualified Person Training course is an instructor-led program designed to prepare GSL Electric employees to safely perform electrical work on or near energized equipment in accordance with OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart K, MSHA §56.12001–§56.12071, and the NFPA 70E Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace. This training fulfills GSL Electric’s requirements for designating employees as Qualified Persons as defined in the company’s Electrical Safety Program.

Through classroom instruction, demonstrations, and discussion, participants will gain a deep understanding of electrical hazards—including shock, arc flash, and arc blast risks—and learn the essential practices and procedures to mitigate them. The training emphasizes safe work practices, hazard identification, and compliance with the hierarchy of risk control methods to reduce potential injury or damage to health.

Participants will learn to:

  • Identify exposed energized electrical conductors and circuit parts and determine nominal system voltages.

  • Establish and maintain Limited, Restricted, and Arc Flash Boundaries as required by NFPA 70E.

  • Select and properly use personal protective equipment (PPE), insulated tools, and testing instruments rated for the voltage and energy level.

  • Perform electrical shock and arc flash risk assessments, including required documentation and job safety planning.

  • Understand and apply the procedures for energized electrical work, including the Energized Work Permit process, pre-task assessments, and lockout/tagout verification.

  • Coordinate with Isolation Officers, Foremen, and the Safety Department to ensure work is performed in an electrically safe work condition whenever possible.

The course also covers the responsibilities of Qualified and Authorized Persons, including decision-making authority, risk evaluation, and communication with host employers during energized work tasks. Participants will review incident response procedures and methods for emergency release in the event of an electrical contact.

Upon successful completion, employees will demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and decision-making ability necessary to meet GSL Electric’s definition of a Qualified Person. Training completion will be documented by the Safety Department and maintained in the employee’s training record in accordance with NFPA 70E 110.4 and company policy.
